NICK GOLDMAN

By: Joy Summers | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
A ground breaking experiment that stores DATA in DNA offers an exciting solution to future humanity

Unique Selling Point:
One on One interview with NICK GOLDMAN

Summary:
Take a look at Nick Goldman’s profile and the published papers under his name, and its likely as a lay person, you would have no idea what this man with a PHD from Cambridge is up to. Fortunately,this mathematician has a very easy way of explaining the groundbreaking research he and his team of scientists and mathematicians are doing. Nick will be in South Africa in November and will do an interview with Carte Blanche.


Further information:
As we become more and more technically advanced we are presented with a problem. Where do we store all the millions of terrabytes of human data? Surprisingly the answer to that question had its genesis in a bar, when Nick Goldman, Head of the European Bioinformatics institute and a few colleagues asked the same question. They began a few drawings on table napkins and soon decided that it was possible to store large amounts of information inside DNA

So they took a photograph of their institution, the famous voice recording from Martin Luther King’s “I have a dream” speech, a PDF document from the men who discovered the double helix, and all 150 of Shakespear’s sonnets. They then invented a code and converted the information into that code. The information was then placed by other scientists into a strand of DNA. Fedics then picked up the parcel and it was sent around the world and arrived back in London at Nick Goldman’s office. He is a mathematician and not a DNA scientist, so when he first opened the test tube, it appeared empty. But in fact, the small smudge at the bottom of the test tube contained all the information and they were able to decode it and voila, all the information was there.

This experiment has huge implications for storage of big data. In fact they have done a calculation and worked out that the entire planets information if stored in this way would likely all fit fairly snuggly in the back of an ordinary panel van. Carte Blanche meets Nick Goldman and tells this incredible story with huge implications for our future.

Press Release:


Nick Goldman’s DNA Storage Idea
Sometimes great ideas are born in odd places. Dr Nick Goldman is a mathematician at the European Bioinformatics
Institute (EBI). This is a repository of cutting edge science and genomic data from around the world. But a few years
ago, the EBI had a problem, their budgets for data storage were being outstripped by the torrents of data they had
to store. One evening Goldman and his colleague kicked around their data storage problem in a bar, and came up
with an idea. Is it possible to store any kind of data in DNA, they asked? Carte Blanche tells the story of their
remarkable experiment that began as just a few random scribblings on a table napkin.

Script:


Nick Goldman FINAL SCRIPT

Commentary One
Have you heard the one about the mathematician that goes into a bar and comes out with a revolutionary idea that could change the way humans store data?

Derek
Nick, is it true that your revolutionary idea started in a pub?
Nick
It is! It was a bar in a hotel in Hamburg

Commentary Two
Meet Nick Goldman, a mathematician, with a PHD from Cambridge in molecular evolution. Recently, he was in South Africa at the BCX Disrupt Summit where he shared his story.

Up Sound Nick

Commentary Three
If there’s a man who understands how DNA can store the secrets of life from thousands of years ago, its Dr. Goldman.

BCX summit Nick
And it’s the DNA in the genome of every living organism.

Commentary Four
He’s published about 100 scientific papers, and now works here at the European Bio informatics institute where raw data about genomes, and the way cells function, is stored

Nick
And we are one of the main world hubs of storing and organizing that data – and making it available to scientists freely over the internet, in addition we have a number of research teams doing fundamental research on computational molecular biology – so how do we use computers to help us understand what is going on in living cells in genomes

Commentary Five
But a few years ago, EBI had a problem. They were running out of space and budget to store the huge amounts of knowledge generated by scientists. Ironically it was data on DNA, they were storing, and DNA is a perfect repository of information, this irony was not lost on Goldman and his director, Ewan Birney that evening in Hamburg.

NICK: And at the end of the day in the bar we said if only there was another way? If only we didn’t have to buy more disks and more cooling systems, and as a joke we said the information we are storing is from DNA, and it’s often called the hard disk drive of a living organism. Couldn’t we use DNA to store information and we looked at each other and said well yes, we could!


Derek
So, you had this lightbulb idea. How did you take it further?
Nick
Well we got napkins and pens out. The lightbulb moment was- we know we can do the reading and the writing

LINK
With every innovation comes an obstacle and in this case not to store the information, but actually to write it in a reasonably fast and cost-effective way

Up sound: Martin Luther King
I have a dream that one day…

Commentary Six
To see if their concept could work, they chose Martin Luther King’s speech, Shakespeare’s 154 sonnets, this photo of EBI, and Watson and Crick’s research paper that first described the double helix of DNA. Then in his spare time, Goldman wrote a code to convert the files into something they could represent in DNA

Derek
now I am nodding my head as if I understand everything but how do you use that molecule to store that data?
Nick
So, we get hold of Martin Luther King’s voice as an MP3. On the computer, essentially that has been stored as a series of zero’s and ones. I wrote a computer programme, and it converts that series of zeros and ones into a series of symbols that represent molecules of DNA. So now I have kind of the design for a piece of DNA

Commentary Seven
Nick then sent his code on an excel spreadsheet to Agilent in California who created the DNA according to his code.

Nick up sound
We get the company to actually make that DNA

Commentary eight
The lab in California then sent it back via Fedex in a test tube

Nick
First time when it arrived, I am a mathematician and not a microbiologist, I was convinced it had gone wrong because they sent me a test tube and the test tube was clearly empty – it arrived on my desk I took it out and there was nothing in there!

Commentary nine
But then his microbiologist friend pointed out a smear in the test tube


Derek: it really is a speck?
Nick: It’s a speck, and the spec of DNA is unthinkably small!

Commentary ten check visuals
The lab read the DNA, Goldman decoded that, and bizarre as it sounds, there were his files spelled out in the DNA.

Nick
I decoded it using the inverse of my encoding procedure and it worked!
Derek
So this spec proved that you were on the right track?
Nick
This spec proved that you could do almost one megabyte of information with zero error.
Derek
Now some of our viewers will be feeling very uneasy now, they are thinking you are going to use our human tissue for computers?
Derek?
We are absolutely not going to do that we have chosen not to do that, so we are using DNA the chemical, it’s a molecule, and the existence of DNA doesn’t imply the existence of life

Commentary eleven
Goldman reckons they are still about ten years away from people using it routinely, but he says, the big tech companies all have teams looking at it. The advantages are obvious- DNA can easily be stored for years in a cool, dry dark place, and it’s compact.

NICK GOLDMAN
So, if we extrapolate that out- all the information in the world stored on all digital devices in the world, that you could fit it into the back of a small truck or an SUV

THE END 6: 00.

PROMO ONE 10 seconds
An idea born in a pub, could change the way we store data
NICK
The actual raw information, everything in the world in an SUV

PROMO TWO 15 seconds
When the European Bio- informatics Institute ran short on storage space, Dr. Nick Goldman and his director, came up with a novel idea
Nick
Couldn’t we use DNA to store information and we looked at each other and said well yes, we could!

PROMO THREE
Derek link
Storing information has been a challenge for mankind ever since we started painting on cave walls

Commentary
Now Dr. Nick Goldman, inspired by DNA’s ability to store data has come up with a revolutionary idea
